statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Neutral. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements apply to “financial institutions” and require reporting of suspicious transactions under Treasury/FinCEN regulations, but the facts do not establish whether Entity SYN_10fbd5b1 is a covered financial institution subject to SAR rules, nor do they provide enough information to determine that any transaction is “suspicious” under the applicable regulatory standards.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates that covered “financial institutions” report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” as implemented by Treasury/FinCEN regulations (i.e., SAR rules). Element 1 (covered entity): The fact pattern describes SYN_10fbd5b1 as a “Securities broker / dealer firm,” which could be a financial institution, but § 5318(g) applicability depends on whether it is a regulated broker-dealer/other covered financial institution under the BSA/SAR regime; the facts do not confirm registration/status, regulator, or that it is subject to SAR filing requirements. Element 2 (suspicious transaction): The transactions listed are large wires/ACHs among LLC counterparties, but § 5318(g) requires suspicion of a possible violation or other SAR-triggering criteria under the implementing rules; the facts provide no indicators (e.g., known illicit source, structuring, sanctions nexus, fraud typologies, customer profile mismatch beyond general volume, or other red flags) sufficient to conclude the transactions are “suspicious” within the meaning of § 5318(g). Therefore, § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements cannot be determined to apply on these facts.
